title: When the mind runs off
hookLine: the hymns often call the mind restless; the practice is only to come back

cards: You sit down. You start the breath and the word. Wahe, Guru.
Wahe, Guru. On the third breath you remember you never answered your sister's message. On the fourth you're planning dinner.
By the sixth you're replaying an argument from 2019, and you've won it this time. Then, suddenly, you notice. Oh.
I was supposed to be doing something. It's easy to read that moment as failure. The Gurus saw it very differently.

teach.h: MAN — THE MIND, RUNNING TEN WAYS.
teach.b: In Punjabi the mind is man, and the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib talk to it constantly, almost like a friend who won't sit still.
They describe it running in all ten directions, chasing one thing after another, never staying in one place.
The Gurus aren't surprised by this. They expect it. That's the first comfort: a wandering mind isn't a sign you're doing it wrong.
It's the normal weather the hymns are written for. The second is how the Gurus speak to the mind. Not only with scolding.
Guru Amar Das addresses it with astonishing tenderness.

teach.h: O MIND, YOU ARE FORMED OF LIGHT.
teach.b: In paraphrase: O my mind, you are the very form of divine light; know where you came from. The restless thing that ran off to your 2019 argument is, in this line, made of light. It isn't the enemy.
It's something that forgot its home. So the practice isn't chaining the mind down. It's only coming back.
You notice you've wandered, and that noticing is itself the moment of simran. Then you return to the next breath and the word, without a lecture. Wander again in ten seconds?
Come back again. A hundred times is fine. Simran is less like building a wall and more like calling a child home at dusk.
You don't shout at the child for playing. You're just glad when they're back at the door.

how: Sikh teachers describe the wandering mind as the normal condition the hymns address, and simran as gently returning attention to the Name each time it drifts.

s: a wandering mind means your simran has failed
the hymns expect the mind to run; noticing and returning is the practice.
a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib calls the mind a form of divine light
Guru Amar Das: O my mind, you are the form of light; know your origin.
the Gurus only ever scold the mind
they also speak to it tenderly, like something that forgot its home.

games.q: you're three breaths into simran and you realize you've been planning dinner for a minute. what do you do?
o: give up: today's not a good day.
scold yourself and start over, stricter.
notice, and come back to the next breath.
games.why: just come back. in the hymns' picture, the mind is made of light and has only forgotten its home; returning is the whole practice.

practice: Start with the breath and whichever word you like, Waheguru or Satnam, or just the breath if you'd rather.

When your mind runs off, notice where it went, name it in one word, like work or food or worry, and come back to the next breath, kindly, the way you'd welcome that child home. See if you can come back three times.

wordCard.voice: Man. The Punjabi word for mind, which wanders in the hymns and is not scolded, only noticed, and brought back.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: man, the mind, which the hymns speak to again and again.

carryVoice: Your line: come back. No scolding, just the next breath. Day one hundred twenty-three, done.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 441 (Guru Amar Das, Raag Asa: man tu jot saroop hai)
